implementation_notes: Scala's channels are the scala.concurrent channels: a scala.concurrent.channels.Channel (an unbounded queue of AnyRef with send/receive/<-/<-, and a SynchronousChannel with no buffer) - the Akka-style API. For the blocking, bounded, thread-safe case, java.util.concurrent.BlockingQueue (ArrayBlockingQueue for bounded) is the more common and better-maintained choice. For the coroutine/async case, fs2 or cats-effect's Queue (cats.effect.Queue.offer/take, with a bounded capacity that blocks the offer via a Semaphore) is the typed, backpressure-aware channel. The select equivalent is cats.effect's select or a race between a channel and a timeout. Termination in Scala's Channel is a poison pill or a shutdown message (there is no close in the unbounded Channel); cats-effect Queue closes explicitly. A key Scala-idiomatic point: channels carry AnyRef (untyped) in scala.concurrent, so the typing discipline of the pattern is only enforced by cats/fs2's typed channels.
idiom_name: java.util.concurrent.BlockingQueue (blocking bounded) or cats.effect.Queue / fs2 Queue (typed, backpressure-aware, closable)
pitfalls: scala.concurrent.channels.Channel is unbounded and carries AnyRef (untyped) and has no close - it does not give the pattern's typed, bounded, closable contract; use cats/fs2 or a BlockingQueue for that.
scala.concurrent's Channel terminates via a poison pill or a shutdown message, not a close() - a forgotten sentinel hangs the consumer.
BlockingQueue.put blocks the thread when full - correct for a thread hand-off but wrong inside a fiber or an effect (block a dispatcher).
cats-effect Queue.close() must be called or the take loop never ends; offer after close fails (which is the correct send-after-close error).
The unbounded scala Channel removes backpressure; a bounded cats/fs2 channel or a BlockingQueue applies it.
alternative: java.util.concurrent.ArrayBlockingQueue for a bounded blocking channel; cats.effect.Queue (or fs2) for a typed, closable channel with backpressure in an effect
